The eggs of the Uniform swiftlet (Aerodramus vanikorensis) are elliptical and relatively small, with a measured length of 20.9 millimeters and a width of 13.7 millimeters. Using the standard formula for an ellipsoid, the calculated volume of an egg yields a predicted initial wet weight of approximately 2 grams [Ww0 = approximately 2 grams]. This modest mass is typical for a swiftlet of this body size and reflects the substantial energetic demands of incubation within the dark, humid caves the species frequents. Available data for a closely related congener, Aerodramus brevirostris, suggest the incubation period under stable cave conditions lasts about 20 days [ab = about 20 days], a duration that has been adopted as a reliable proxy for Aerodramus vaniko at a temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C]rensis. Notably, this reported developmental period of 20 days is specifically linked to an incubation temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C], which is cooler than typical avian incubation temperatures and may contribute to a slightly lengthened embryonic development phase.

Following successful hatching, the nestling phase is characterized by rapid somatic growth fueled by intensive biparental provisioning. The newly hatched chicks, weighing approximately 2 grams [Ww0 = approximately 2 grams], must accumulate substantial mass to reach the adult size required for independence. Sexual maturation occurs relatively early in life for a bird of its size. Based on data from Aerodramus brevirostris, a model species for cave swiftlet life history, puberty is attained at approximately 81 days after hatching [tp = approximately 81 days after hatching] when the ambient temperature is maintained at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This onset of reproductive capability marks a significant physiological transition. However, the time from birth to the first successful brood is delayed to a full year, recorded as 365 days since birth at first successful brood [tR = 365 days since birth at first successful brood] under the same thermal conditions of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], indicating that while gonadal maturation is rapid, the behavioral and ecological prerequisites for nesting are not met until much later.

The fledging event, when the nestling attains flight capability and departs the nest, is a critical milestone in the life cycle. For Aerodramus vanikorensis, this stage is inferred from comparative studies on the congeneric Aerodramus brevirostris. The available evidence suggests that the time since birth at fledging is 27 days since birth at fledging [tx = 27 days since birth at fledging] under the typical active-phase body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This relatively short nestling period is characteristic of small, aerial insectivores that rely on high metabolic rates and rapid feather development to reduce predation risk within the nest. After fledging, the young birds are still dependent on their parents for provisioning for a period, gradually learning to hawk insects on the wing before they achieve full nutritional independence.

The maximum reproductive rate observed in the Uniform swiftlet is constrained by its life-history strategy. Field surveys indicate that females lay a clutch of 1 to 2 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 1 to 2 eggs per nesting attempt], a typical number for cave-nesting swiftlets that face high energetic costs of foraging and chick rearing. Furthermore, these birds typically produce only a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], resulting in a low annual reproductive output. This reproductive pattern is characteristic of a slow life-history pace, where parental investment in a relatively small number of offspring is prioritized to increase the probability of survival for each young. The active-phase body temperature during these critical reproductive activities is maintained at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], a thermal state that facilitates the high metabolic demands of egg production and chick provisioning.

The energetic physiology of Aerodramus vanikorensis is characterized by a heightened metabolic rate, a necessity for its continuous aerial foraging lifestyle. Respirometry trials conducted on wild-caught individuals have established a maximum basal metabolic rate of 21.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 21.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the subject is in a post-absorptive, resting state at a core body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This relatively high metabolic intensity is consistent with other small insectivorous birds that maintain a high wing-beat frequency and elevated heart rate during flight. The maximum lifespan for this species, based on known records and population models, is estimated at 14 years [am = 14 years] at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. Adult body mass is sexually dimorphic, with females reaching an ultimate wet weight of 10.8 grams [Wwi = 10.8 grams], while males are slightly lighter, attaining an ultimate wet weight of 10.5 grams [Wwi = 10.5 grams]. This subtle difference may be linked to the energetic burden of egg production on females.
